name: Valman
confidence_why: Schmidt 1900, the only description of Valman (Walman) that marks accent, places it on the penultimate syllable in most words with numerous marked exceptions, and Spölgen and Schmidt 1901 by the same author only adds that verbs usually stress their initial prefix syllable, so the penultimate reading rests on one century-old missionary source that no later work (Brown and Dryer 2008 is silent) confirms or contradicts.

new_statements.translation: e) Accent: It falls in most cases on the penultimate syllable, but the deviating cases are numerous enough; they will be marked by the accent sign ´.
new_statements.citation: Schmidt, P. W. (on material collected by P. F. Vormann S.V.D.). 1900. Ein Beitrag zur Kenntniss der Valman-Sprache (Neu-Guinea). Zeitschrift für Ethnologie 32: 87-104.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. Opened (18 pp., scan of ZfE 32, printed pp. 87-104). Rendered PDF page 2 = printed p. 88 (header 'P. Vormann und P. W. Schmidt') at 150 dpi and read the image: under '§ 1. Die Lautverhältnisse' item 'e) Accent: Derselbe fällt in den meisten Fällen auf die vorletzte Silbe, doch sind die abweichenden Fälle zahlreich genug; sie werden durch das Accentzeichen ´ kenntlich gemacht werden.' The quote is there verbatim (the text/scanned also carries it, with 'Acceutzeichen' as an scanned error only). Same page: 'járien = schlagen', 'jákälä = ziehen' with acute on the first of three syllables, and p. 98 (PDF page 12) word lists show marked accents on several words in…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent is penultimate by default; exceptions are frequent enough that the author marks them with an acute in the word lists (e.g. járien 'to strike', jákälä 'to pull' on the same page, both with non-penult marked accent). Given the stated frequency of exceptions, a reader could also file this as lexical (unpredictable) with a penult default.
new_statements.exceptions: Yes: 'die abweichenden Fälle [sind] zahlreich genug' — deviating cases are numerous and are marked with an acute accent; no rule given for them.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (Lautverhältnisse of individual words in a missionary sketch; citation forms in the word lists); 1900 field material by Vormann after one year at the Valman station, written up by W. Schmidt, who calls the material 'lückenhaft' (fragmentary).
new_statements.identity_note: The 1900 sketch describes 'Valman' spoken on the coast opposite Tumleo/Seleo/Ali islands (Berlinhafen, German New Guinea), i.e. the same Walman/Valman of Lemieng village documented by Brown & Dryer (they cite the same missionary tradition, Becker 1971) — valm1241 itself, no dialect named. The source spells the language Valman.

new_statements.quote: [p. 358] Fast durchgängig haben die Verbalformen den Accent auf der ersten, der Präfix-Silbe. Für alle übrigen, welche denselben meist auf der zweiten Silbe haben, plädiert P. Spölgen mit Entschiedenheit dafür, dass sie als zusammengesetzte Verben zu betrachten seien, zusammengesetzt aus nan ‚sein', und einem Substantiv oder Adjectiv. [p. 360] Wo sonst noch Verben mit dem Accent auf einer anderen als der ersten Silbe sich finden, liegen andere Zusammensetzungen vor, so ist näago ‚thun' = nä ‚geben', ‚bewirken' + ago ‚fertig', ‚beendet'. [p. 356] Das Präfix vo ist stets tonlos.
new_statements.translation: [p. 358] Almost throughout, the verb forms have the accent on the first syllable, the prefix syllable. For all the others, which mostly have it on the second syllable, Fr. Spölgen argues decidedly that they are to be regarded as compound verbs, compounded from nan 'be' and a noun or adjective. [p. 360] Wherever else verbs with the accent on a syllable other than the first are found, other compounds are involved; thus näago 'do' = nä 'give', 'cause' + ago 'finished', 'ended'. [p. 356] The prefix vo is always unstressed.
new_statements.citation: Spölgen, P. N. & P. W. Schmidt. 1901. Beiträge zur Kenntnis der Valman-Sprache. Wiener Zeitschrift für die Kunde des Morgenlandes 15: 335-366.
new_statements.locator: Part B 'Beiträge zur Grammatik' (Schmidt): §8 Verbum, p. 358 (extract PDF page 24; volume PDF page 369) and p. 360 (extract page 26); adjective section before §7, p. 356 (extract page 22); 'Accentverschiebung' p. 362 (extract page 28). §1 Lautverhältnisse in this paper (p. 351) adds only d) Auslaut and e) Lautwandel; no accent subsection. Quotes checked against the page scan.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (32 pp., text present; extract page N = printed p. 334+N). Extract page 24 = p. 358 reads: 'Fast durchgängig haben die Verbalformen den Accent auf der ersten, der Präfix-Silbe. Für alle übrigen, welche denselben meist auf der zweiten Silbe haben, plädiert P. SPÖLGEN mit Entschiedenheit dafür, dass sie als zusammengesetzte Verben zu betrachten seien, zusammengesetzt aus nan ‚sein', und einem Substantiv oder Adjectiv.' Extract page 26 = p. 360: 'Wo sonst noch Verben mit dem Accent auf einer anderen als der ersten Silbe sich finden, liegen andere Zusammensetzungen vor, so ist näago ‚thun' = nä ‚geben', ‚bewirken' + ago ‚fertig', ‚beendet'; ebenso wird näkälä ‚ziehen' eine Zusammensetzun…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's penultimate rule and the 1900 statement ('in den meisten Fällen auf die vorletzte Silbe, doch sind die abweichenden Fälle zahlreich genug'): the 1901 paper incorporates that statement by reference and adds a morphological account for verbs (accent on the prefix syllable; second-syllable accent = compounding), plus the unstressed vo- prefix and one accent shift. Its trisyllabic initial-accent verbs (nórolo, nókoro) are among the marked exceptions the 1900 rule already allows; it does not claim initial accent for the language as a whole.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Verb forms only: the accent falls almost without exception on the first syllable, which is the subject-prefix syllable (n-/v-/y-/m-/k- + stem); verbs whose accent sits on the second syllable (nanápi 'speak', nanáre, napáro 'help', napálo, namímo, numíe, nurúkül, nataraú 'steal', novóyue 'be bad') are analysed as compounds of na(n) 'be' + noun/adjective, and näago 'do', näkälä 'pull' as compounds with nä 'give'. The paper states no general word-accent rule of its own: p. 335 n. 1 refers the orthography (including accent marks) and p. 350-351 refers the sound section back to Schmidt's ZfE 1900 p. 87 statement, which it explicitly does not repeat. Disyllabic verbs (napu, mapu, kago, yago, nätä) make initial = penultimate; trisyllabic verbs with initial accent (nórolo 'seek', nókoro, p. 362) are antepenultimate, i.e. the kind of exception the 1900 paper said it would mark with ´.
new_statements.exceptions: Verbs with second-syllable accent explained as na(n)-compounds (p. 358-359) or nä-compounds (näago, näkälä, p. 360); the prefix vo- is always unstressed, and vóyue 'bad', vónulo 'younger brother' with accent on vo are explained by contraction of vo-óyue, vo-ónulo (p. 356); 'Accentverschiebung' nrŏlo, mrŏlo from nórolo (p. 362-363); ei-forms (meipu, neipu, keigo, yeigo) found only in the talk with the Vrinagol men, possibly a dialect difference (p. 360).
new_statements.identity_note: Both papers describe the Valman of the Berlinhafen (Aitape) coast opposite Tumleo, Seleo and Ali, from the SVD mission station (Vormann's notes in 1900; Spölgen's texts and letters in 1901, Spölgen died 2 March 1901 and the station was abandoned). The 1901 paper notes ei-forms of some verbs occurring only in a conversation with 'Vrinagol-Männer' (p. 345, 360), which Schmidt suspects may be a dialect difference. No later phonological source (Brown & Dryer) was in this work list; the ELAR Walman deposit remains unopened.

readall_conflicts: No contradiction between sources. Schmidt 1900 (ZfE 32: 88) gives the general rule: accent in most cases on the penultimate syllable, with numerous marked exceptions. Spölgen & Schmidt 1901 restates nothing general (it defers to 1900 for orthography and §1) and describes verb accent morphologically: almost always on the first, prefix syllable, with second-syllable cases treated as na(n)- or nä-compounds. For the disyllabic verbs cited the two descriptions coincide (initial = penult); for trisyllabic verbs with initial accent (nórolo, nókoro) the 1901 verb generalization picks out exactly the 'abweichende Fälle' the 1900 rule allows, and for trisyllabic verbs with second-syllable accent (nanápi, napáro, namímo) the surface placement is penultimate. The tension is one of framing (morphological prefix-accent for verbs vs. a default penultimate count), not of data.
